content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its recommendations for the treatment of adolescents and children with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. These updates also include simplified service delivery and diagnostic approaches. A survey was conducted to gather the values and preferences of healthcare workers who care for children and adolescents with HCV. The findings of this survey were used to inform the updated guidelines. The survey was designed to target healthcare workers who have experience caring for children and adolescents with HCV. Data collection was managed using the REDCap electronic data capture platform, which is a secure, web-based software designed to support research studies. The survey was validated in consultation with the WHO Paediatric Working Group on Viral Hepatitis and was distributed in English. Recruitment for the survey involved networks such as the Penta Foundation, pediatric gastroenterology and hepatology societies, and WHO regional viral hepatitis focal points. A total of 142 individuals responded to the survey, but the analysis focused on 94 respondents who had provided care for children or adolescents with HCV in the past three years. These respondents, referred to as experienced healthcare workers, represented all WHO regions. Most of them were pediatricians, pediatric infectious disease specialists, or pediatric hepatologists, and the majority worked in tertiary care centers. They reported substantial experience in pediatrics and/or viral hepatitis care. The experienced healthcare workers reported a cumulative total of 1,799 children and 2,253 adolescents with HCV under their care over the past three years. The largest number of cases was reported from the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region, particularly from Egypt, where some respondents had cared for over 700 children in the past three years. On average, each healthcare worker had cared for 43 children, with most having cared for fewer than 25 children during this period. Regarding treatment experience, 87% of the experienced healthcare workers had treated at least one child or adolescent with HCV in the past three years. The majority of these treatments involved adolescents aged 12–17 years, with fewer treatments reported for younger children. Only 2% of respondents had treated children younger than three years old. Sofosbuvir combined with ledipasvir was the most commonly used drug regimen across all age groups, followed by sofosbuvir combined with velpatasvir. In terms of drug availability, 22% of healthcare workers reported that no drugs were currently available at their facilities for treating children and adolescents with HCV. This issue was most prevalent in the Western Pacific and South-East Asia regions. Among facilities where treatments were available, the most commonly available regimens were sofosbuvir + ledipasvir, sofosbuvir + velpatasvir, and glecaprevir + pibrentasvir. Funding for pediatric HCV treatment was primarily provided by government or public sector sources (60%), followed by self-funded patients (25%). A smaller proportion of funding came from private insurance (10%) and non-governmental organizations (2%). Healthcare workers identified several key outcomes as important when considering whether to treat children and adolescents with HCV. These included achieving sustained virological response (SVR12), minimizing long-term adverse effects, preventing transmission to others, and reducing the stigma associated with HCV infection. Preferences for treatment varied by age group, with a focus on ensuring effective and accessible care for all affected children and adolescents.
